name: cw (Rust wc replacement)
baseline: wc from FreeBSD base (C) and GNU coreutils 8.30 wc (gwc, C)
workload: Counting bytes, lines, words, characters and max line length of a 341,152,640-byte XML file (Dickens_Charles_Pickwick_Papers.xml) and of test-utf-8.html, single file and many files via xargs; timed with hyperfine-style 'times faster' output.
claimed_speedup: README, per flag set versus wc / gwc: cw -l 3.44x / 4.17x faster; cw -lL 1.73x / 15.07x; default (cw with no flags) 1.45x / 2.05x; cw -m 70.36x / 30.21x (XML) and 84.74x / 124.21x (test-utf-8.html); cw -mlL 9.05x / 3.88x (XML) and 9.42x / 18.95x (HTML); cw -mLlw 3.15x / 1.35x. Many files with xargs and --threads=12: 11.55x faster than wc and 17.31x faster than gwc.
compiler_and_flags: cw built with 'cargo build --release --features runtime-dispatch-simd' (recommended in README); baseline build flags and Rust version not stated; gwc is GNU coreutils 8.30.
why_faster: README: line counts use the bytecount crate (SIMD, runtime dispatch), line-length mode uses the memchr crate, -m has a UTF-8 character-counting fast path, and --threads counts several files in parallel. The author notes gwc is pessimised in places by FreeBSD's weak memchr.
tradeoffs: Byte-oriented unless -m; ignores locale (no locale support yet per README Future list); UTF-8 only; no test suite listed at time of README; word counting uses a slow path.
caveats: First-party numbers from one 2021 FreeBSD 12 VM-class machine; the main baseline is FreeBSD's base wc, not GNU wc on Linux; gwc is penalised by FreeBSD's memchr per the author. The -m rows compare a UTF-8-only counter with wc's locale-aware multibyte path, so they are not equal work, and the --threads row uses 12 threads against single-threaded wc. Repo untouched since March 2021.
found_via: crates.io API keyword scan ('memchr', crate cw 0.7.0); README Performance section opened via raw.githubusercontent.com and the github.com repo page

name: huniq (Rust sort | uniq replacement)
baseline: GNU sort -u and GNU sort | uniq -c (coreutils; versions not stated); also awk, GNU datamash and the earlier C++ huniq1
workload: Removing duplicate lines (and, in -c mode, counting them) from /usr/share/dict/* concatenated 1 to 100 times, timed with the unix time tool via benchmark.sh.
claimed_speedup: README unique mode: huniq2-rust 0.26 s vs 'shell' (sort | uniq) 7.30 s at 1 repetition, 3.40 s vs 93.75 s at 10, 43.65 s vs 1062.07 s at 100; README text 'Compared to sort -u: huniq is around 30 times faster' and 3.5x to 6.5x faster than the C++ huniq1. Count mode (-c): 1.47 s vs 7.71 s at 1 repetition and 90.80 s vs 933.67 s at 100, text 'between 5x and 10x faster than sort | uniq -c'.
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release (README Build section); sort/uniq/awk/datamash versions and flags not stated.
why_faster: README: hash tables / hash sets instead of sorting the input ('Sorting is slow').
tradeoffs: Output is in first-occurrence order, not sorted; memory is much higher than sort | uniq (29.5 MB vs 9.7 MB in unique mode, 132 MB vs about 12 MB in -c mode per README tables); -c output order is unstable.
caveats: First-party, hardware and tool versions unstated; the win is algorithmic (O(n) hash set against an O(n log n) external sort) so it is not a like-for-like language comparison and does not hold when sorted output is wanted; the memory cost is 3x to 11x. The README's 'shell' row is sort | uniq with default locale settings that are not stated.

name: runiq (Rust duplicate-line filter)
baseline: GNU sort -u and uniq (coreutils; versions not stated); also uq and huniq
workload: Filtering duplicate lines from 25,000,000 JSON documents (1.9 GB, 20.67% duplicates) and 100,000,000 documents (7.7 GB, 55.69% duplicates), sorted and unsorted input, output to /dev/null.
claimed_speedup: README table, 25M lines unsorted: runiq -f quick 12.1 s and 298.7 MB vs sort -u 380.2 s and 8.33 GB (about 31x faster, derived from page data); sorted input: runiq -f sorted 10.3 s vs uniq 24.9 s (about 2.4x, derived). 100M lines unsorted: runiq -f quick 34.7 s vs sort -u 2529.9 s (about 73x, derived); sorted: runiq -f sorted 24.9 s vs uniq 105.8 s (about 4.2x, derived). huniq is about equal to runiq (11.9 s and 31.2 s).
why_faster: README: filters that use hash sets, a bloom filter ('compact') or a streaming sequential check ('sorted') instead of sorting the whole input; memory and speed optimised.
tradeoffs: Compact filter is probabilistic; simple filter uses 2.3 GB to 5 GB of memory; sorted filter only detects adjacent duplicates, like uniq.
caveats: The author says the numbers are a reference for his own tuning, 'not meant to be a competition'; no hardware, compiler or tool versions are given; unsorted comparisons are algorithmic (hashing against sorting). The sorted-input uniq comparison is the like-for-like one.

name: encodify (Rust Base64, Base32 and Quoted-Printable codecs)
baseline: simdutf (C++) Base64 codec, called through the simdutf Rust crate
workload: Criterion throughput (GB/s) of Base64 encode and decode, MIME Base64 with 76-column CRLF lines, Base32 and Quoted-Printable at 32 B, 1 KiB, 64 KiB and 1 MiB (cargo bench --bench codec).
claimed_speedup: README, 64 KiB, against the fastest other crate: Base64 encode 25.7 GB/s (1.0x simdutf) on Apple M5 Max NEON and 19.2 GB/s (1.0x base64-turbo) on AMD EPYC Zen 2; Base64 decode 18.1 GB/s (1.2x simdutf) and 15.0 GB/s (1.0x base64-turbo); MIME encode 21.3 GB/s (1.5x simdutf, LF only) and 10.7 GB/s (1.1x simdutf); MIME decode 14.1 GB/s (1.4x simdutf) and 8.6 GB/s (1.7x simdutf). Plain Base64 is parity with simdutf; at 32 B the Apple M5 MIME-encode row has simdutf (LF only) ahead, 5.75 GB/s vs encodify 4.50 GB/s, and base64-simd decodes 32 B faster than encodify (7.73 vs 6.08 GB/s).
compiler_and_flags: Criterion via 'cargo bench --bench codec'; rustc version and the C++ build flags of the simdutf crate are not stated (README shows RUSTFLAGS cfgs only for the AVX2-off and scalar variants).
hardware: Apple M5 Max (NEON) and AMD EPYC Zen 2 (AVX2)
why_faster: README: SIMD kernels for NEON and SSSE3/AVX2 with runtime detection, output appended to caller-owned buffers or slices without zero-filling or hidden reallocations.
tradeoffs: Mail-protocol oriented API (RFC 2045, 2047, 2152, 3501, 7468); SIMD only on NEON and x86 SSSE3/AVX2.
caveats: Brand-new first-party repo (published 2026-10-02) with 3 commits. The C++ baseline is the simdutf crate wrapper, and the simdutf rows are 'LF only' for MIME, so they do not emit the CRLF output encodify produces. Plain Base64 is parity, so the real wins over C++ are the MIME rows (1.1x to 1.7x). Outside the MIME case, base64-turbo and simdutf are within a few percent.

name: awkrs (Rust AWK)
baseline: mawk 1.3.4 and GNU gawk 5.4.0 (C); BSD awk on macOS also timed
workload: hyperfine on 1,000,000-line inputs: '{ print $1 }', sum of first column, multi-field print, regex filter, associative-array count, conditional field print, field arithmetic, string concatenation, no-match gsub, plus a CPU-bound BEGIN loop.
claimed_speedup: README tables (mean ms, awkrs vs mawk vs gawk): { print $1 } 15.7 vs 66.2 vs 100.8; sum first column 13.0 vs 37.5 vs 62.9; multi-field print 56.4 vs 156.6 vs 266.1; regex filter 11.1 vs 19.3 vs 351.4; associative array 340.0 vs 610.0 vs 342.4 (parity with gawk); NR%2 field print 30.2 vs 71.1 vs 116.1; field computation 19.0 vs 57.7 vs 100.5; string concat print 51.0 vs 121.0 vs 182.2; CPU-bound BEGIN loop 9.2 vs 9.7 vs 20.7.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (cargo release build); mawk and gawk builds not stated beyond versions.
why_faster: README: on regular files a raw byte path parses the Nth whitespace field straight from an mmap'd buffer, a 'slurp inline' path does a byte memmem scan for gsub, and a fused-superinstruction bytecode VM runs the rest; optional rayon parallelism (-j, default 1) and a fusevm/Cranelift numeric offload that does not engage on these string/field programs.
tradeoffs: Not a full gawk (documented parity gaps: interactive debugger, extension loading, multibyte field splitting not audited); parallel mode only for parallel-safe programs.
caveats: First-party, single machine (macOS arm64), whose mawk/gawk are probably distribution builds; the fast paths read regular files through mmap and skip the VM, while the baselines read through their general record loop; the README's own 2026-06-01 caveat says the JIT rows come from a Cranelift module that has since been removed. Parity only on the associative-array case. The repo has 1 star and no third-party reproduction.
